title: World War One's Pearl Harbor?
text:
If we remember anything at all from our high school history class about why the United States got into World War I, it might have something to do with unrestricted submarine warfare. But the Zimmermann Telegram, if it was even mentioned, has long disappeared from memory, along with most of the other "facts" we learned in school. Barbara Tuchman, in this superb little book, makes a strong case for the argument that it was the revealing of the contents of this one message that convinced the American public that war with Germany was necessary.

The account reads like a spy thriller, which in fact it is. But there is not one statement which cannot be documented. Tuchman had access to American, British and German records which clearly illustrate the process of decision-making for each of the governments involved. The author has a knack for encapsulating her view of the often unimpressive character of the major players.

By 1916 World War I had degenerated into a horrible bloody stalemate from which there was no escape. Each side was desperate for fighting to end, but could accept nothing less than defeat of the enemy. None of the belligerents were prepared to consider Wilson's efforts toward "peace without victory." The only solution for the Allies was to bring the United States into the war, and for the Central Powers, to keep her out. Germany was convinced that, through unrestricted submarine warfare, against neutral as well as belligerent shipping, she could force Britain to capitulate in a few months. The Allies were hoping for a German blunder that would finally drag the U.S. into the war, and Britain did have a secret weapon of which the Germans knew nothing; she had broken the German diplomatic code and was reading all German international messages, both cable and radio. How this all played out is the theme of this little volume. It is illuminating, with respect to this important turning point in world history, and to the processes by which nations are governed.

"Life is a Strange Place" is the fourth published novel for Frank Turner Hollon; an Alabama lawyer turned author. title: Exceeded My Expectations In Every Way!
text:
Reign of Shadows exceeded my expectations in every way and kept me on my toes the entire story. Danger around every corner, romance, and adventure had me loving every second of Reign of Shadows. I was seriously hooked until the last sentence, and I defiantly did not want it to end there. Luna is an exceptional heroine in this novel, even with her disadvantages she is stronger and tougher than most of the other survivors left in her world. I could not help but want to root for her in every way.

There is a bit of romance, and I love that it does not come out forced as sometimes I find other book will do just to have a romance aspect to the story. It has a natural feeling to it, and it even acts like a beacon of hope in a world of eternal darkness. With switching points-of-view, readers get to experience the story from both Luna’s perspective and Fowler’s perspective. I have always been a fan of the multiple viewpoint stories, as I think it provides a 360 view of the story and the characters. I think it is a needed feature in Reign of Shadows as these two characters both have many thoughts and secrets that only readers get to experience through the changing perspective.

The setting and world building of Reign of Shadows is perfect. It is a dark and creepy world where dark dwellers rise up from the ground every day to eat anything living and without any real sunlight, survivors of the eclipse on get one hour of peace when the dark is just bright enough to drive the dwellers back underground. The description of the dwellers were detailed enough to nearly give me nightmares after reading Reign of Shadows.

This is the first book of Sophie Jordan’s that I have had the chance to read, but I have always heard amazing things about her other books. Now I know that I have definitely been missing out, and I am setting to rectify that mistake as soon as possible. Her writing sucks you deep in the story and holds you there until the very end brings you back to reality. Only the truly best stories can offer that type of hold over a reader.

title: Outstanding book on grief
text:
Out to Sea is the kind of book I wish I had had for my daughter when my own mother — her nana — died. Death is a hard concept, especially for young children. And memories are fleeting. It was less than a month later that my daughter said she couldn’t remember Nana’s voice. It’s been three years, and most of the memories are gone, but we still find Nana in my daughter’s smile, in our garden, in books and in our hearts.

Out to Sea explains all this in such a simple and profound way. Helen Kellock’s sparse text and encompassing illustrations speak right to child’s — or adult’s — heart. And while exploring social and emotional issues, Kellock’s use of color and movement is exceptional. I highly recommend this book for families going through the grieving process.

It was stolen and returned more times than I could count—lost and then found even more than that. I’m convinced that this pencil has the life span of a styrofoam cup in a landfill. Buy this pencil, because you’re buying more than a pencil here: you’re buying something that you could quite possible carry through an entire era of your life. title: The kind of book that you'll be reluctant to finish.
text:
Ever since the quality of Elizabeth George's books took a nosedive, I've been searching for another favorite mystery author. I've found her. And interestingly, like Ms. George, Deborah Crombie is an American woman who sets her mysteries in England.

The book has three threads: one is the ongoing romantic relationship between Superintendent Kincaid and his partner, Gemma James. A second is the mystery itself, involving a beautiful woman whose body is found carefully laid out in a park. The third is the genesis of the relationship among some of the characters/suspects and their families, a relationship which began back when English children were transported to the countryside to spare them the horrors of the World War II Blitz.

All three themes are handled beautifully. The characters of Duncan Kincaid and Gemma James continue to develop believably throughout this series. (This is, I believe, the sixth Kincaid/James book). The real-life problems and uncertainties they encounter while trying to maintain their family and professional obligations, and leave time for themselves and each other, will strike a believable chord with anyone old enough to have gone through this phase of life. The mystery is complex and unpredictable enough to be challenging but not confusing. The ending is beautiful - it settles both the mystery and the unresolved pain from the events of the 1940's.

If you haven't discovered the Crombie/Kincaid/James series yet, I recommend starting with the first one, "A Share in Death," which was nominated for an Agatha as best first novel of 1993. But I've read all of the first six, and they're all excellent.

title: A fun way to explore language
text: This is a book I would have loved to have as a child. It's not the kind of book you just sit down and read cover to cover, it's more like a very specialized dictionary. The author has curated a list of words--four for each letter of the alphabet--and explains how it is used and how it came to be used. As the author notes in the introduction, words have personalities, and this book explores them. Did you ever wonder why a British policeman is called a Bobby? Why the yellow weeds we see everywhere are called dandelions? Why long races are called marathons or why it's called a quarantine when people are kept separate from others? This book explains all these words and many more, including some that are definitely not in the average grade school vocabulary. Although the book is published in the United States, there are many words used more commonly in Great Britain and a fair amount that may seem a bit archaic, but readers still learn about everyday words like pajamas and shampoo. It's a great choice for encouraging creativity, enlarging and enriching a child's vocabulary, and for that kiddo that just loves knowing all sorts of off-beat and fascinating facts. Grownups reading along with them should be prepared to be surprised and educated, too.

title: Do you dare read Chacour's book?
text:
During my second reading, Elias Chacour's _We Belong to the Land_ continues to draw me in with its imagery, challenging message, humor, and engaging observations about the Holy Land. I have studied the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, traveled the West Bank and Galilee, and met with Israeli leaders, and yet, Chacour's text provides insight into the complexity of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict and the plight of indigenous peoples of the Holy Land that no amount of studying or traveling could provide.

If you consider yourself pro-Palestinian, I challenge you to read this text. If you are pro-Israeli, Christian Zionist, or Jewish Zionist, I challenge you to read this text. If you are serious about understanding the challenges we face in resolving the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, then I challenge you to read this text.

And I promise, you won't regret it.

https://smile.amazon.com/Sunlite-Flat-Form-Excerciser-Pedals/dp/B000AO5J5W/ref=sr_1_1?s=sporting-goods&ie=UTF8&qid=1492112707&sr=1-1&keywords=exercise+bike+pedals

UPDATE 08/12/2018 REPLACED BELT

After about a year of daily use I noticed a black powder accumulating on the ground under the belt cover. I figured out it was the belt wearing out. I purchased a new one (OEM PN 5PK1320). I couldn't find any instructions on the Sunny site but it's not that hard. Remove all the screws from the belt cover, including the one that holds it in place on the left side of the bike. You might have to remove the right pedal to get the cover completely off. Once you have the cover off, remove the 10-mm retaining nuts on the two eyebolts that align the flywheel, then loosen the two 19-mm nuts that hold the flywheel in place. Lift the flywheel far enough up to slip the old belt out and the new belt in. Align the belt on the front pulley and reattach the 10-mm eyebolts to the frame, then tighten the 19-mm flywheel bolts. Place the belt on the back pulley as far as you can get it, then turn the crank to get it on the rest of the way, the same way you get a chain back onto a bicycle chain ring. Put the cover back on and you are done.

text:
Another good read book.
People who expect too much will be disappointed (like some of the reviewers), but people who just want a good read will like it.

It has drama, good battles, plausible technology and decent characters.
Why would his enemies want to still get rid of him even though he keeps winning? I find that totally plausible and even likely, people are not logical and they can be jerks just for the sake of being a jerk and once they've decided that someone is the enemy, it might require them to admit they were wrong and far too many people can never do that.

I would not say that this is the best book in the series, but I awaited it eagerly and finished it in one sitting without being bored.

It's a good read and possibly trite and predictable (you know the good guys are going to win, but, well, duh. As if you thought that Sauron was going to get the Ring back too).

As for the aliens, I'm gonna have to disagree that they are setting up another series, there is something in this one that seems to explain why the aliens are doing what they are doing. There have been hints in other books (book 3 had a bunch) that make them look not necessarily like bad guys. But that's just my opinion.

I hope Campbell does more books, but I just don't see him setting up another series with a war against the aliens.

title: Alamo Questions
text:
Chariton explores a number of questions revolving around the tragedy of Alamo. Most of the questions he explores are, in fact, not legends but legitimate questions as to what did or did not happen in an around the time that the Alamo was attacked and the defenders slaughtered. Generally I agree with Chariton's deductions although I also believe that all testimony regarding the Zuber must regarded with extreme suspicion. Zuber claimed that he got his information from Louis Rose, the supposed only deserter from Alamo. In a manner resembling Thucidides, Zuber admitted embellishing [making up] Travis' final speech to the troops, including the famous 'line in the sand'. In my opinion, if Zuber lied about anything, then it should be rightfully assumed that he lied about everything.

I think Zuber's testimony is an insult to all the men who died at Alamo. Their heroism stands by itself and required no second hand editorialism. I'll go even further than that to proclaim my own belief that Louis Rose--if he ever existed--never testified to Zuber. Zuber made up the entire story 'whole-cloth'.

Ron

title: A real treat to Adrien and Jake fans, and a love letter from Josh Lanyon to these beloved characters.
text:
A very entertaining, thought-provoking, occasionally emotional read.

Fatal Shadows, the first book in the Adrien English series, being so well known to Josh’s readers, seemed like the perfect choice for a Choose Your Own Adventure version, because the characters and their original trajectory are so familiar that it becomes easy for readers to experiment with and explore even the wildest alternative scenarios,
The book also presents some new characters and some unexpectedly tender moments involving them,
Moreoever, some of the most satisfying storylines in this book are IMO those where a little more is subtly revealed of a character’s emotion and thought than in the original book. It has a liberating effect, as the CYOA concept allows a lot of freedom to uncover all those fears or bottled up emotions that in the original Fatal Shadows had remained under the surface,
The illustrations by Catherine Dair are the icing on the cake :). They make the book richer (and only a print edition could do them justice) and it’s a nice nod to the original CYOA book format which includes illustrations. And they’re not just there for decoration: Josh uses them as a plot device, so they can’t definitely be missed :)

All in all, I didn't expect such a rich and inventive book. What I did expect, and was not disappointed with, was the apparently effortless way Josh Lanyon has to combine humour, dry wit and emotion in such a creative and satisfying way.

I think if I could characterize this bag with one word, it would be "sturdy".  The leather of the bag is thick and feels like it could last several life times.  Even the fabric used in the interior feels thick and durable enough to last forever.  I'm not a huge fan of the green interior, I would've preferred a deep blue or red but that doesn't factor into my review, its just a personal preference.  The shoulder strap feels ok, not bad but not great either.  The shoulder strap works fine but doesn't feel as well built as the bag, but this is a tiny problem.  I'm also happy to see legitimate straps for the side compartments and not magnetic clamps on the bag.  I was sick of the magnets because they become undone far too easily.  The threading of the bag looks and feels great but only time will tell how well the threading will hold up.  One small gripe is that because of the fact that it is hand made, it will have some degree of variability.  This has lead to the flap that overhangs the opening to feel a little "loose" and the position of the handle coupled with how the leather is creased makes the weight of the bag pull more on one side than the other (the weight pulls more on the back of the case than the face of the case).  I'm hoping that this dissipates once the bag is broken in.  Overall, I still think it is a fantastic buy, especially considering the price.  With all the features considered, I'd give it a 4.5 out of 5 but they only allow reviews in equal increments, so I'll give the case the benefit of the doubt and assume that the threading on the case will last as long as the leather.  5 out of 5.

title: First impressions from a first-time Hardshell user
text:
I've used Gatorskins for years, riding my Specialized Tarmac SL2 in the hills surrounding the San Francisco Bay Area. The shoulders of these near-urban backroads tend to be strewn with debris and there's plenty of shattered glass remnants from long-ago broken bottles. (No street sweepers set foot on these roads!)

Even though I've got a fancy lightweight racebike, I put up with the added rolling weight of Conti's Gatorskins because when I used to ride with "racing" clinchers, I'd get two or three flats a month. And I hate fixing flats! Spoils the rhythm of my ride!

My last set of Gatorskins lasted two seasons. This time, when ordering replacements, I opted for the "Hardshell" version. And let me tell you, there's a difference in the riding experience. The hardshell component is a thick layer of solid rubber over the middle of the tire. When inflated at the recommended pressure (110 psi), I'm feeling every bump and pebble I ride over quite a bit more than was my experience with regular Gatorskins. My sense is that the thick rubber in the center is reducing the bump-absorbing effects that make pneumatic tires essential on most vehicles.

No doubt as these Hardshells tires wear, the ride will become less stiff. And I wouldn't be surprised if all that extra rubber gave me an extra season's life from my set of tires. But I've got to say, I miss the shock absorbtion of my regular Gatorskins. When the time comes to replace these Hardshells, I'll probably go back to the non-Hardshell Gators. They gave me all the flat protection I needed and provided a comfy ride as well.

title: A pleasant read, but could have been much better - 3.5 stars
text:
Meet the Essex sisters: four Scottish ladies recently orphaned and left impoverished with no prospective husbands. Now wards of the perpetually inebriated Duke of Holbrook, their first mission is to marry off their eldest, the witty and sensible Teresa, or Tess, as she prefers to be called.

Growing up without the proper training that other ladies of their kind receive, Tess knows that she must marry in order to support her sisters. But what she didn't expect is that she will immediately catch the eyes of two very eligible English gentlemen. There is the Earl of Mayne, who seems to genuinely like her and whom she will most likely develop a nice, though not passionate, affection for; and then there is the very rich, though just a mere Mister, Lucius Felton, who unnerves her and whose very nearness makes her heart somersault. While Tess knows that either man is a good choice, she is torn when both men ask for her hand in marriage.

While the story started off with a great promise, the focus on establishing the characters of the four sisters overshadows what could have been a really delightful romance between Tess and Lucius. Just when you think we'd finally get some action going between the main characters, the heroine would be involved in her sisters' dramas and so the focus is once again taken away from the romance. However, the interactions between Tess and Lucius when we finally get to the part are rather sweet, and at times, funny. The little banter we get to see between them surely adds to the delight of the story.

Overall, MUCH ADO ABOUT YOU is a pleasant read and holds promise for the stories of the other Essex sisters. Next are KISS ME, ANNABEL (Annabel's story) and THE TAMING OF THE DUKE (featuring Imogen).

title: It is like having a conversation with her
text:
Full disclosure: I have met Angelo Lowery at a writer’s retreat in Sedona Arizona. Angelo is in person, as she is portrayed in her memoir, “I am and the Spirit Walks with me,” a force to be reckoned with.
When I met Angelo, it was the first time in my life I met someone who has a direct line of communication to God. Her eyes are full of light, and she exudes a natural sense of strength and power. Reading her book, it was a surprise to me to hear all that she has endured in her life – abuse, betrayal, stunning loss. And yet, in her life, she has been able to rise above the pain to directly touch God. She has turned betrayal into blessing, loss into communion and pain into healing.
Angelo’s book is imperfect, as are many self-published books that do not have the benefit of a high-rolling publishing house behind them. But in its imperfection, it is perfectly Angelo. It is like having a conversation with her. She writes as she speaks, in a lovely, sometimes innocent, sometimes all-knowing, inspired and warm tone….until she speaks the words she hears from God. It was fascinating to read how distinctly different were the voices of her book – hers versus God’s.
Angelo is a warrior, she has survived countless horrors that would crumple the best of us. How did she do that? She shares that she always knew she was somehow chosen by God to do special work (Angelo is a gifted healer today). Was this the key to her resilience? For many who suffer adversity, their experience becomes an excuse to visit adversity on others. For Angelo, it became an opportunity to draw close to God and heal both herself and others.
I would love for Angelo to share next how we mere mortals, those of us who have not felt chosen, can also rise above adversity in our lives to become a conduit of good and love and spirit as she has done. Thank you for sharing your heroin’s journey, Angelo.

text: As an educator and the mother of three now-grown children, I read most of the books about trends in teaching and education reform that come out every year. Mostly I am disappointed because the books are way too theoretical or they whine about problems without suggesting solutions. Or they just rehash the same ideas. So I was thrilled to read Voices from the Classroom. The author frames the sad situation in our public schools in a new and different way. title: Decent product, good price, functions as advertised
text:
tl;dr version: For $32 you can't go wrong.

I've been using this backpack cooler almost daily since I bought it two weeks ago. I use three, small rectangular "blue ice" packs placed on the bottom, on top of a small, folded dish towel to absorb any condensation. I haven't used it with ice. Some reviewers say the top zipper leaks if you use ice that melts. I can well imagine...so don't use ice.

There is plenty of room in this thing for enough food and drinks for two or three people. It's kept me fed through a few double shifts and everything stays cold for a good 20 hours. The blue ice packs are still half-frozen after that long. I live in a temperate part of the country, I can't say anyone in Arizona or Nevada, for instance, would have the same results, so caveat emptor.

The straps are long and wide enough to be comfortable when wearing this as a backpack, and I'm a pretty big guy. It also carries well slung over one shoulder, which is not always the case.

Some of the reviews fault the zippers for breaking. Yeah, I can see that happening if you jerk them, are impatient, or in a hurry and not paying attention. I've had no problems with them. Same with the stitching; I pack out at about 20 pounds and I've seen no signs of wear and tear, yet. It has only been two weeks, sure, but still...

Pros: keeps food plenty cold for a whole day when used with re-freezable ice packs; lots of room inside, comfortable straps. Netting pockets for water bottles, etc. on the sides are deep and big enough for wide bottles.

Cons: zippered storage compartments on the front and top are inadequate. No "waterproof" storage compartment for keys, phone, etc.

After actually getting it and trying it in person, (a) it looks even classier than the photos, and (b) it's got a nice heft and rigidity to it that gives it a feeling of quality I was not expecting. It really is a brushed aluminum piece there, not shiny plastic. Admittedly, it's expensive, but after trying it out I don't think it's disproportionately so.

About the trackpad ("TouchDisc"): I noticed some reviews commenting that it's nothing special. That's partially true; for the most part, it works just like normal laptop trackpad, which is good. The scrolling support has an interesting feature, though: on normal rectangular laptop trackpads, you place your finger at the right edge of the trackpad, and move it up and down to scroll. But you soon hit the top or bottom edge of the trackpad and have to stop. On the diNovo Edge you start the same way, by placing your finger at the right edge, but because it's round you instead move clockwise or counterclockwise to scroll, so you never have to stop. So once you start it scrolling you can just keep spinning your finger in circles around the outside edge over and over, pause, or change direction. The speed and accuracy of this approach are both big improvements, particularly when scrolling up and down long pages.

As for Linux support: no need for special drivers for the support of the main keys or the touchpad. In fact, many of the special media keys worked as expected out of the box, including the volume slider. Depending on what you're using to map keyboard shortcuts, though, not all of the media keys were available to be mapped without some tweaking. For these, a program called "keytouch" (probably available in most package managers) let me program the rest; it included settings for a different diNovo keyboard that seems to work fine for the Edge and includes most of those other keys already.

title: Good, even-handed account of Davis' flight
text: The Long Surrender is a good book with the wrong title, because Jefferson Davis certainly did not surrender.  This book chronicles the events beginning in April of 1865, when Lee surrendered and Richmond fell.  Jefferson Davis and his entourage fled with the remaining treasury.  The author gives a well-researched and even-handed account of the flight of Davis.  It captures his determination to somehow rally the remaining forces and continue the war, despite the advice of his generals.  I bought this book because I wanted to understand Davis better and learn what is known about his postwar days.  It's a bit dry, but nevertheless interesting.  Davis spent two long and miserable years in confinement, and was treated inhumanely by his captors.  It recounts the anguish of his wife and her efforts to obtain at first better treatment and finally his release.  The book is chock full of little known facts about this dark period of history.  It gives a fairly detailed accounting of the Confederate treasury and the personal funds of Davis.  There is no glossing over the flaws in judgment and intransigent attitute of Jefferson Davis, but the book also illuminates his courage, conviction, and many good qualities.  For those who want to see the bitter end of his "presidency" this book is a must.

title: Twisty Rods for Beachy Waves or Coily Curls
text:
My hair has lots of different kinds of curls in it, from tight coils near the nape of my neck, to spirals, all the way to slightly wavy hair at the crown of my head. I get a more consistent curl when I use curlers! I've been using large foam curlers for a while to get large, uniform waves that straighten out over a few days, but I wanted to try a curler that would give me tighter curls.

The Ohuhu Twist Flex Rods come with 7 different curl sizes, and each size has 6 rollers. The rollers are color-coded by size, so you think I'd be able to find all 7 curlers, but apparently I thought there were only 6 when I took the picture. I'd never used these kinds of curlers before, but they were simple to use. I used the two largest sizes, and took a small section of hair and put the end of it in the middle of a roller. Then, I rolled the hair up into the roller, making sure to keep the hair in the center of the rod. Twisting the ends together keeps the curler in place.

I tried to let my hair air-dry with the curlers in, but I have a LOT of hair, and knew that could take days, so after a few hours, I put on my bonnet dryer and finished the job. I was pretty happy with my ringlets! I did muss them up for a nice, beachy curly-wave, too. I really liked getting the curl all the way to my crown, and how much lift it gave the top of my 'do. And, the curls weren't tangly like my hair can get if I let it completely air dry. I could run my fingers through them and get a messy, beachy wave - and still no frizz or tangles.

title: Skillful, witty and caring
text:
I was delighted to find this author, known for his travel narratives and splendid prose, an Englishman born in 1908 and only dying recently at age 95 in Saffron Walden, Essex, where he had lived modestly and politely, shyly even. Luigi Barzini described reading his prose as "like eating cherries" and Graham Greene - with whom Lewis shared many similarities in adventures, courage and quiet, commanding prose - had "no hesitation in calling him one of the best writers, not of any particular decade, but of our century".

In this work - part of a multiple volume autobiography, there was only one decision Lewis made that damaged his intellect in this readers view - he agreed to an investigative reporting trip to Peru accompanied by Lord Snowden as his photographer, traveling "incognito". Lewis seemed genuinely surprised that was far from a successful trip, or experience, and as for the `incognito' - well at least it got the author free upgrades to First Class flights and entertainment by British Ambassadors and Peruvian society!

The author had a fascinating and often wildly exciting life, serving in the British Forces in Italy during WWII followed by a career in journalism reporting on Vietnam, Burma, Indo China and producing a splendid series of books for Jonathan Cape - who used to entertain his authors with dinners of burnt Irish Stew - on the mafia in Sicily, and the threatened indigenous peoples of Latin America.

Writing with a compassion and light wit Lewis crafted over thirty books and one of his five children, his second son Gareth, has also published a book called 'Deceit'.

title: Incredible life — even to a layman like me
text:
First let me preface this review by saying that you should NOT be turned off to this book if you know nothing about physics or mathematics. The author does an incredible job at explaining the semantics of Diracs theories while only seldom mentioning any syntax (his explanation of the delta function was impressive).

Now on to a life worth remembering. This book does an incredible job at commemorating not only the achievements of Dirac (along with his contemporaries, always making sure credit goes where credit is due) but also the person that was Dirac. You know it’s a good book when an author makes you feel as if you knew the bloke, even though he died before I was even born and lived across the globe.
The author meticulously builds up the image and story of Dirac, with no page going to waste. I know — a book about one of the most abstract theoretical physicists to ever live, how could this be fun? Read it and prepare to be surprised!

This book not only helped fill my knowledge gaps within the history of mathematics, but also provided days of thorough entertainment.

I would recommend this book to anyone interested in the history of mathematics and one of the pioneers of Quantum Mechanics.

10/10

text:
I held on to an old box of Swingline size 11 rubber fingers from 20 years ago, and started using them at work finally almost 2 years ago. I love them.

I just finally wore out the last one (I only had 6 to start with), and ordered these as replacements. They are horrible - not even remotely close to the original product. I ordered both size 11 & 11.5, because I recently ordered the Acco brand size 11 from Staples, and they were too small. These Swinglines are identical to the Acco brand from Staples - they are the same product, if anyone is wondering, except the size 11 I received from Amazon are even smaller, and the 11.5 are too big for my finger. Really - a half size varies so wildly that neither of them fit my index finger.

I am just going to assume that they are making them as cheap as humanly possible and have no desire to have any level of quality control, nor care about the comfort of their product. The rubber doesn't even have a tack to it, unlike the old ones I have. The new ones might not stretch out, but to me, that is not a plus. I would rather have a fingertip that stretches over time, but at least it works for several months of daily rigorous use before it finally wears out.

I must now search for another product that might suit my needs, or try to find an old box on ebay - which is always a gamble, and not a permanent solution.

I miss the old days wear quality mattered - I can't buy a children's game, or even a t-shirt - that has any quality craftsmanship about it. I'm really tired of cheap and crappy stuff.

What a waste of time. I'll keep limping along with my stretched out fingers as long as I can - or maybe I can gain 50 pounds, gets fat enough to fit inside the ones I have.

title: More like "Helping Badger Overcome Depression"
text: I was surprised to see this book so breezily reviewed.  I myself found it disturbing.  There are lots of good books around that deal with bad moods--"Alexander and the Terrible, Horrible, No Good, Really Bad  Day" and "Today I Feel Silly & Other Moods That Make My  Day" come to mind.  This book goes way beyond moodiness and knocks on  the door of clinical depression.  First, the animals find Badger sitting in  his chair in the dark.  When they switch on the light, Badger snaps at them  to turn it off and leave him be.  The other animals leave, but Mole is  worried about Badger so he stays and cleans up the place a bit. Badger  eventually speaks: "I'm sorry about this. 'Spect I'll get over it.  But right now, I'm just no good, you know.  No good for anything."  Mole tells him they'll "just wait".  Eventually the animals call  a doctor.  Badger refuses to see her and sends Mole out to get rid of her  and the other animals trying to help:  "Close the curtains," he  begged Mole.  "Keep them away."  Then we have a scene where Mole  watches Badger "staring and dozing and turning heavily in his  chair."  YIKES! And then, just when you're sure Mole is going to be  calling the suicide hotline, things turn rosy and child-appropriate again.  Mole comes up with the idea of an Awards Ceremony (this causes Badger's  eyes to move "sharply for the first time in days").  Badger and  all the other animals attend.  Badger wins all sorts of awards for being a  good person/badger.  At last he feels "appreciated" and is happy.  Everyone dances.  I was confused (and creeped out).  My child was  confused:  "How come he wants to sit in the dark?...How come he  doesn't want the doctor to help him?...Doesn't he like the other animals  anymore?...Does he like them better now that they had a party for  him?"  If this had been a book to help children understand  depression--a book with an appropriate resolution and ending--it would have  been fine.  If this had been a book about a badger who was feeling glum and  unappreciated, who was then cheered up by an awards ceremony, it would have  been fine.  But this book is a bizarre marriage of the two and it is AWFUL.

As a text in college focused on China this would be my first choice, supplemented by outside readings in Chinese history, culture, politics and global finance. The text covers the essential strategic commercial China background and questions - the why China, why now, and what is unique and relevant - - then takes a disciplined process approach to how you enter and manage in China. From the essential "entry" mode, alliances, partner selection, negotiations and more. Critical topics like managing HR in China, from a distance - motivation and more. The topics touch reality and are enriched with proven theory - backed with case studies, analysis and numbers.

The language is easy to read, follows threads to conclusions, coupled with insightful learnings backed with contemporary in country examples - getting the point is easy - sensible - and retainable. This is a fluid and masterful presentation and not at all a dry, nor choppy mashing of fact, example, and anecdote together. Easily in my top 10% of China reads on business.

When it comes to daily tasks for me, it's mostly web browsing and streaming with light gaming mixed in a few times a week. I play Overwatch, CS:GO, Path of Exile, Rust, Diablo 3: RoS, GTA V, and a few others. Load times are definitely quicker with an SSD compared to a traditional HDD. From pushing the power button to desktop takes about ~11 seconds.

I don't do heavy data transfers, so I don't reach the true potential of this drive, but I wanted to invest in the longevity and dependability with Samsung. Just be careful when looking at M.2 SSD's. NVMe's aren't compatible with certain (older) motherboards. I made that mistake when I went to buy another 970 EVO for my laptop (HP Pavilion 15). The laptop was only compatible with M.2 SATA SSD's and not NVMe's.

text:
Someone else gave a review saying they couldn't get these bottles to spray. The bottles I received have a screw type nozzle. Tighten the screw and it will spray a fine mist. Loosen the screw nozzle and it will spray a heavy stream.

The bottles are semi-transparent and have graduations on the side in ounces, milliliters, and a neat feature in the middle called "dilution ratio". It makes sense when you see it.

All 3 of the bottles I got came with the red handle/nozzle/neck. So I used my label maker (also purchase from Amazon) to ensure I don't get the three chemicals mixed up.

In the past I've used cheap junky spray bottles that leak out the handle when you squeeze them. I have NOT had that problem at all with these.

I use these bottles to a variety of tasks around the house. One is filled with bleach for aggressive cleaning, such as the bathroom or to kill mold growing outside my house. One is filled with a home-made cleaning mixture of equal parts rubbing alcohol, vinegar, and distilled water (works great on glass!). And the last one is diluted hydrogen peroxide used to treat indoor and outdoor plants. Hydrogen peroxide will break down quickly when exposed to light, so make sure you store it in a dark/cool/dry place.

title: Great for documents.  Horrible for photos. Get it on sale and it's a steal!
text:
If I could do it, it would be 3.5 stars. Here is the skinny:

Pros:

Scanning and printing of normal documents is great.

You can scan to a network folder, your computer, to FTP, to a USB stick, or email as an attachment right from the printer. It's more than reasonable for first page out and multiple pages.

Easy setup. Printing from your phone is easy. Internet printing capability (print from anywhere, ready when you get home).

Toner is like all color laser printers, relatively expensive for the brand name but much cheaper than inkjet in the end.

Have been successful faxing using a OBI200 and a Google Voice number so very handy when you need to occasionally fax but don't have a physical land-line in the house.

While it isn't silent, it is not unreasonably loud. My old Canon inject makes more racket (clicks, clacks, bangs) when it starts up.

I have never had wake from stand-by issues. Wakes from sleep pretty fast.

Cons:

It is big (small con). But all color lasers tend to be in this size and up as they need to be able to hold and align all those cartridges. As a matter of fact, due to the pull-out tray design and smaller physical cartridges this is probably on the smaller side of color laser printers.

Flatbed color scanning from your computer of things like photographs, is IMHO HORRIBLE, with out of whack colors and edge diffractions and all sorts of oddities. It's to the point that I wonder if it's defective. Oddly, scanning of documents seems pretty good. I need to do some experimentation to see if it's a software driver issue or something but I've scanned direct into Photoshop, Picassa, and Acrobat and they all are pretty sub-par. The computer driver scanning controls are now very basic, not like they used to be years ago with much more control...maybe that's part of the problem.

Also, when _printing_ photographic type images the colors are massively over-saturated...okay for presentation graphs, charts, and stuff but again waaaayy off base for anything else. While I understand this is a business oriented machine, even businesses scan/print photographs and it shouldn't be this far off (a lack of functionality/settings in the printer driver could be partly to blame).

title: Pictures without much explanation
text:
I have a lot of ambivalence about this book. In some respects I'd give this 1 star and others i'd give it 5, so I split the difference and gave it 3 stars.
the good: The photographs themselves. You can see 2 examples of a scene and how Sam handled them differently.
the bad: I found the writing incomplete. It was like the attitude was, "Isn't it obvious? The photos speak for themselves!" and I don't think they do.
In some cases I thought both pictures were great and couldn't figure out which one was supposed to be better. In other cases I wondered, "What are people seeing? What makes this great?" and I found no help from the book.

After getting the book I saw a lecture by Sam on YouTube. It was about an hour long and he had many of the same photos in it. But in the lecture he explained what his goal was, what his approach was and why the final photo was the one he liked best. I thought this would have been great info to include in the book and wonder why it was not there. (OK, maybe it is obvious to everyone else in the universe and I just didn't get it. Totally possible, but I do have a strong visual arts background...but photography seems to play be different rules and it was not clear from this book what they are).

With Sam's lecture in my mind I like the book a lot better. But it seems odd that it did not work as a stand alone item. (at least for me, who had no experience with his working methods and goals when I first got the book).

Would I recommend buying it? Yes. But with the caveat of watching some YouTube lectures by Sam, if you are not familiar with his work and what makes it great.

title: The Birth of a Conservative Movement
text: I have to say that this is one of the few books that I have read that has explained a subject in a way that has radically changed the way I think about a subject. While many critics have pointed to the adoption of the "Southern Strategy" by the Republican Party that has allowed them to gain control of the South, I can think of no other author that has explained it in such a methodical and clear way and with a crucial  distinction.  In fact Kruse argues that what has been characterized as that Souther Strategy is in fact a Suburban Strategy.  The main point of the book is that much of the modern day conservative movement can trace it roots back to the resistance to integration in the late 50's, 60's and 70's  and that Atlanta and its metro area is the perfect example of this shift that occurred nation wide.  What makes this book so good is that it does not assume anything and traces the events in very meticulous detail describing the constantly shifting alliances in the black/white coalition in Atlanta and the though processes on both sides of the issues and while I personally found it very difficult to be sympathetic to those wanting to maintain the status quo,  after reading this book I could see how they got to the ideological point that they re now.  This book is a must read for anyone interested  in the History of political movements in American and the south especially!

I did a ton of research before buying this keyboard, i was in the market for a gaming mech keyboard (i even picked this one over the stealth, price diff aside).

I also like the 5 macro keys down the left side, they are within easy striking distance and add more keybinds (which insane that i need more, i do have a Naga mouse lol). The back lighting is great as I prefer to play in the dark, and the lockout of the windows button is also a great feature (long nails clipping it during PVP is BAD). The included editing software is easy to use.

As for the sound, is it loud? Yea a bit, obviously it's louder than a normal keyboard, but I actually enjoy it, and joyfully clack the keys. It's really not that loud, maybe if you were in a empty room with high ceilings were it could echo would you find this a issue. I dont really see any gamer that is enough into gaming that they would A. want a mech keyboard, and B. pay this much for a keyboard having an issue with it. Just don't try using it in the same room your GF is sleeping...

Improvements/cons? Wish you could adjust the back light levels and color, and maybe 5 more macro buttons by the space bar would be lovely (i'm sick i know). The ONE con i do have, its that sometimes my space bar sticks, its VERY VERY rare- and i can't say that is actually a design flaw- it could be a cookie cumb or something... heh. So, i wouldnt suggest nibbling on something around it.
Great job Razer. Oh and btw, when i've had issues with past items (naga mouse addon being buggy), the razer tech guys were amazing and intense about figuring out my problem (Screen shots etc).

title: Good Protection
text:
I am quite pleased with the iSkin Duo. It is a tight fit, but as a result it keeps the iPod from slipping out. The case consists of two pieces: the tight skin with a clip that goes directly on the iPod (and covers all but the screen and headphone input and port), and the hard case that hugs the front of the skin/iPod and covers the screen.

The clip:
-It has no spring, so I am not sure how long it will last without snapping.
-It seems that you can not separate the clip from the skin without damaging at least one of them.
-It only has 180 degrees of rotation, so you can't turn it upside down (I prefer one that has 360 degrees, but for most this is probably not an issue)
-It does not rotate easily. If you wear pants that are made with light material, when you attempt to rotate it, you will end up just twisting your pants. But for those that prefer it not to move around, this is a good thing.

The case:
For the most part it fits the iPod quite well. The only exception is the hole for the "hold" switch does not line up. Turning "hold" off is not a problem. Switching it on, though, takes a little bit of effort sometimes (emphasis on "little").

This also comes with a a lanyard attached to a plug that fits into the port. This can be used instead of/as a backup to the clip.

All in all it is a good product, and I would definitely recommend it.

It was a privilege to read this book. The writing was bracing and the experience harrowing. By all rights, as awful as many of her trail experiences were, it could and should have been even worse.

To me, this book is a powerful reminder about the importance of taking on the near-impossible task/experience and facing down one's demons.
It is the journey of the hero, but told by a woman who felt like anything but when she set out.
Yes, she was horribly underprepared to trek the PCT and it was nuts to do it solo, and some of the confident hikers who commented scathingly can't forgive her that.
People who hate Elisabeth Gilbert of Eat, Pray, Love for leaving her perfectly sweet husband to "find herself" abroad will probably hate Cheryl Strayed for similar crimes, including self-indulgence.

But I found this a very powerful book. One that I expect to be thinking about for many years. One that I expect, and hope, will influence my own life.

title: Cute Counting Book With Wonderful Illustrations
text: The best thing about "10 Turkeys in the Road" is indeed the turkeys, along with the rest of the illustrated material.  The artwork is superb - colorful, whimsical, and downright funny.  In this counting primer, a farmer's path becomes blocked by 10 turkeys.  The frustrated farmer tries everything to move the turkeys out of his way, but can manage to clear only one turkey at a time from his path.  Preschooler's will undoubtedly love the winsome pictures, and engaging them in the turkey counting shouldn't be difficult.  If there is any criticism to be made, however, it would be the slightly less engaging poetic narrative.  Another well-known counting book, "Five Little Monkeys Jumping on the Bed," offers a significantly more memorable poetic experience by way of it's almost sing-song verse: "Five little monkeys jumping on the bed, one fell off and bumped his head; mama called the doctor and the doctor said, 'No more monkeys jumping on the bed!'"  I've read that one with both of my kids over the years, and the catchy rhythm & rhyme of its language make it a classic.  This book doesn't quite match that one with it's poetry, but the superb illustrations make it worthwhile.  A fine choice for little ones working on their counting skills.

title: The candles themselves look and feel like REAL wax candles - because they are
text:
Wow! This is a very well thought out and fully functional product! Well done! The candles themselves look and feel like REAL wax candles - because they are! It just doesn't get any better. Some things to consider ...
1. As stated, because the candles are made from real wax, you can use "melted" wax to anchor the candles solidly in your candle holders so they remain straight and stable like you normally wood. Great!
2. These wax candles are actually "hollow cylinders" with a removable metal inner cylinder that houses the two AA batteries that power the flame apparatus at the top. This is significant because when the time comes to change the batteries as needed, you can simply pull the inner cylinder out of the wax casing from the top and then simply slide it back in the wax casing. The beauty of this comes from the fact that the wax cylinder remains firmly anchored in your candle holders so you don't have to scrap the melted wax in the cups and re-set them. Very, very convenient!
3. The included remote works terrifically! If you want to conserve battery life you must manually "push down" in the flame top (just like clicking a ball point pen) to completely shut them down and must "click them on" again for your next use.

Bottom line, the flame is not the same as having the real thing but given all of the pluses and convenience, these candles are by far the next best thing. To the makers of this product, it's time for WHITE (and more) candles! I'd buy two sets today!

This DORAMI Spaceship Solar Power Radiometer is fragile and should be kept away from little hands - being made of glass with a partial vacuum inside it's as breakable as an old-fashioned light bulb. title: Afghanistan through the eyes of a child
text: A war-torn country plagued by violence.  An 11-year-old girl forced to risk her life and save her family. These are the realities in Deborah Ellis' novel "The Breadwinner" (Groundwood Books 2000).  Told from young Parvana's perspective, the story focuses on her family of six living in Kabul, Afghanistan.  After the Taliban take control of their city, Parvana's family is forced out of their large home by a bomb explosion and into a one-room apartment.  The women are removed from school and forced to stay in the house unless escorted by a male.  When Parvana's father is arrested because he attended university in England, their family must make the tough decision to have her pose as a boy in order to leave the house and work in the marketplace to earn money for food.  While working, Parvana runs into Shauzia, a girl she knew from school who is also posing as a boy to support her family. They start to work together and soon become close friends, encountering a number of sobering, scary situations along the way. Though children may not experience the same life, they will no doubt relate to Parvana's story and her arguments with her older sister, unfairness of chore responsibilities, and love for her family.  The Breadwinner is not a happy story with a happy conclusion, but one that will leave the reader with a different view of Afghanistan, as seen through the eyes of a child.  An author's note and glossary of terms serve as a helpful aide in introducing children to the history and culture of Afghanistan.

title: A Lighter and More Romantic Cornwell
text: According to the blurb in the front of the book, Bernard collaborated on this book with his wife, Judy Cornwell under the name Susannah Kells.  What resulted is a book that has all of Bernard's customary attention to historical detail, primarily told from the perspective of a much younger and idealistic viewpoint than his typical protagonists- a girl named Dorcas (Campion) Sythe. While the general romantic template is present (i.e. girl falls in love, girl thinks love is impossible, girl fights for love, etc) Cornwell's talent for intricate plot lines, complex villains, and sudden plot twists are present as well.  There were a few times in reading when the sudden switch from Campion's rosy love-filled perspective to a more jaded viewpoint (usually ending in someone's sudden and brutal death) was a little jarring, but on the whole it was still the type of read I expect when I pick up Cornwell's books- A little softer around the edges maybe, but still crafted with his trademark knack for historical realism and ripping good yarns.

title: This debut novel is a delight to read
text: This debut novel is a delight to read, from start to finish.  The characters are richly drawn and come alive quickly.  The geographic settings (Manhattan and the SC Lowcountry) are great contrasts and are vividly drawn bu an author who obviously knows both and knows them well.  The continuing struggle of life in the arts is a key part of the drama that centers around a college grad who heads for NYC in the early 70’s to make it as a dancer.  Her journey is full of twists and turns and some major surprises.  The finale of the book tempts the reader to skip ahead to find out what happens!  But don’t do that.  Go with the narrative and its flow and savor the richness of how things unfold.  While the charms of the south are here, that is nicely balanced by vivid descriptions of lower Manhattan in the 70’s. I hope the author plans a sequel.

title: A near perfect model of an iconic attraction!
text:
This is a really well done Pop! Town set. Clean paint lines with a perfect Mickey. The box was a bit dinged up but that doesn't matter too much to me. The execution of this set is great save for a slight color mismatch between the words "SPACE" and "MOUNTAIN," due to the former being green plastic and the ladder being green paint on grey plastic. Not a huge deal, but I think it's worth pointing out.

My main criticism is with the design. The mountain itself is stretched vertically more than it should be. This is normally fine, Funko stylizes a lot of things right? But with the other Disney World/Disneyland structures they've done, the proportions have been pretty close. Sleeping Beauty Castle and the Haunted Mansion had no stretched proportions at all, so it does make me want a wider more realistic portrayal of Space Mountain here. Again, it's fine for what it is, but it does make me wonder why they stretched this out when the other structures aren't.

title: Great for sharpening knives - a little hard to hold on to
text:
I really like this kit - especially for the price. I have always struggled with getting a perfect edge with a sharpening stone -- I'm just not that good at keeping the blade at the right angle I guess. This kit makes it super easy to keep the same angle throughout the sharpening process - I have gotten razor edges from 30 degrees (my pocket knife) down to 17 degrees (my expensive Japanese kitchen knife) with ease.

There are three minor things I don't like about this kit:
(1) It's pretty hard to grip while sharpening. I usually just place it at the edge of a table with the blade edge facing the ceiling... I've tried other ways, but this works the best for me. Maybe I'll buy a clamp one day to add to it, but for now I'll just deal with it.

(2) The blade clamp left marks on my pocket knife. After that happened, I wrapped some electrical tape around the clamp and that resolved the issue.

(3) The blade clamp doesn't have marks to show how far down the blade is placed... so you can end up with a blade placed differently between 2 sharpening sessions. I haven't found a good solution for this yet, but I'm thinking of making some small nicks on the side of the clamp so I can make notes of where I put different blades - if I do this I'll probably upload a picture to show the change & describe how hard it was to implement.

title: Perfect OEM Replacement (+ install instructions) for Parkside TR-14FT-COMBO
text:
Parkside TR-14FT-COMBO
100% OE Replacement

If this is your trampoline, this mat is a perfect replacement for the original in thickness, stitching and quality of nylon tabs and galvanized rings. The only difference is the branding printed on the center and a vinyl cover over the stitching to protect from UV (better than the original being replaced from 2008).

You WILL need a spring tool and at least a second set of hands to install (or at least hand you springs). And the mat will seem too small at first.

TO INSTALL:
(read through all steps before starting)

NOTE 1: Counting mat rings / frame holes accurately is essential. Get off by 1 and you have to start over.

NOTE 2: Be careful to pull springs straight out (and keep an eye on it as you're pulling) from the mat ring to the frame hole so that the spring stays hooked in the point of the ring. Do not allow the spring to slip to one of the sides or a cascade of problems will ensue.

1) Select a ring on the mat and attach a spring to it and to the trampoline frame

2) Count 42 rings around on the mat and attach another spring

3) Count 42 holes around on the frame and attach the other end of that spring

4) Count 21 rings from either spring and add the next spring; do the same for holes and attach

5) Repeat step 4 on the opposite side

(You now have 4 springs attached at each of the 90º points, creating 4 quadrants)

6) In your first quadrant, count 10 rings and holes from a spring and attach another

7) In the quadrant directly across from your first, count 10 rings and holes and attach another

8) Repeat for the other 2 quadrants

9) Now start filling in the gaps, alternating to the opposite side every couple of springs. The idea is to keep alternating sides so that the tension remains as even as is possible.

***It might seem easier to just start working your way around, but the pull will become uneven, increasing the likelihood of having a ring slip.***

Feel free to message me for any further info.

title: Diplomacy, work, humor, and adventure in this fine memoir
text:
This is Richard Williams' fascinating and wryly humorous account of two years as the U.S. Consul General in the Chinese city of Guangzhou (formerly called "Canton") from 1979 to 1981. His was the first American consulate to re-open in China after formal diplomatic relations with the PRC were established in 1979.

Readers interested in the development of U.S.-China relations will be fascinated -- and entertained -- by this book. Large strategic and foreign policy considerations moved China and the United States to establish relations. It was left to Foreign Service Officers such as Richard Williams and his team to make it all work -- first by setting up a new Foreign Service post, then by issuing visas, establishing commercial relations, traveling through China to report on local conditions, introducing the Big Mac, and escorting the first waves of American visitors.

Americans who know the more open China of the twenty-first century will, in this book, encounter the China making its first hesitant steps toward modernization and reform. The difficulties confronted by early official travelers, the lingering suspicion of America, the obfuscation of officials high and low, and the choices made by Foreign Service families before there were international schools are all described. Williams' wife Jane had left Tianjin as a girl; her reunions with family members in the PRC add poignant touches to the book.

This is a fine book for any young person thinking about a Foreign Service career. Although almost three decades have passed since Richard Williams and his family opened the post in Guangzhou, "At the Dawn of the New China" captures much of the enduring qualities of Foreign Service life.

text:
Amy Gentry's novel, GOOD AS GONE, shares a lot of its plot with other movies and books. It also shares similarities with the true story of the kidnapping of Elizabeth Smart, from her bedroom at night.

A good portion of the story deals with the fallout that is created in the remaining family members when a child goes missing. The part that is similar to other works of fiction deals with how the family copes, when the hoped for miracle happens: the child returns to the family many years later, eliciting both joy and suspicion. The suspicion is driven by thoughts that the returning child (unrecognizable, after so many years) may, in fact, be an imposter.

GOOD AS GONE has excellent, well developed, realistic and sympathetic characters, and a surprise ending that sets it well apart from novels that have come before. The dialogue and family dynamics feel realistic and the author paces it well and keeps you interested and guessing. I enjoyed it.

title: Modern pulp SciFi, with a lot of fun
text: This book is a throwback to the good old days of scifi, with lots of weird aliens, some (fairly) heroic protagonists and a (sort of) quest. The characters are well-drawn, and individual, but they are archetypal, the quest is rather mundane but needed, and the world building is relatively believable. The biggest difference from the earlier pulp fiction is that humans are the least and most recent of the members of the governing Galactic Commons (the GC) with other aliens having much better technology, more advanced civilizations, and a bigger impact on the universe. Humans are acceptable, but it is obvious we are often just tolerated in this world. It is a different take, and an interesting one. I liked the people, I enjoyed the story, and the exciting bits were fine. There is not a lot of back story on how humans became a part of the GC, or what happened to Earth and why humans came to be wandering around seeking a new home, or how they were discovered by the aliens; it is a given from the start. The nine member crew of the Wayfarer contains 5 humans, the owner, two techs (one mechanical, one comp), a clerk, and a fuel specialist (algae is used, and it requires a full-time person to monitor the vats to keep it going); three alien members, a reptile pilot, a bug-like medic/chef, and a fur-covered navigator; and a sapient AI that basically runs the ship. The interactions of the crew and their friends make up much of the book, with some of their backgrounds giving more history. It is a fun read, and I enjoyed it, I was also pleased that there were going to be other books in the series. If you enjoyed the good old days, read this book.

title: Best of the pre-PEP or pre-W series works
text:
Perhaps because of a lack of publication or perhaps because of a general lack of distribution of his ideas (Peirce tended to write only for other philosophers and logicians), Peirce's philosophical thinking was not well known until Eisele's "New Elements of Mathematics" (NEM), and the Peirce Edition Project's W series: "The Chronological Writings of Charles Sanders Peirce". Buchler's work is easily the best introduction to the work of Peirce prior to the availability of NEM and the W series.

Buchler worked from an earlier collection of Peirce's writings, called the CP series, consisting of 8 volumes of poorly edited papers presented in such a way as to not show the depth, or originality of his thought, or the evolutionary growth in the depth and power of his thought.

Nevertheless, Buchler's volume is still an excellent, easy to read, and easy to understand (relative to Peirce's depth of thinking) introduction to the immensity of the thought of Charles Peirce. I recommend it as a great reading value.

text:
Note: I have read the story on RoyalRoad, which goes beyond the currently published books. This review stands as a synopsis of what I have read so far.

Fantastic story heavily inspired by Vampire: The Masquerade, showcasing the unnatural dominion of vampires over humans and most other magical creatures. This includes the existence of distinct vampire clans with unique supernatural traits and an inveterate hierarchical vampire society to maintain power and secrecy.

As the main character, Ariane is painfully reborn into a warrior bloodline with an antediluvian psychopath for a progenitor. Abandoned and left to fend for herself, she must navigate the perils of vampire society as an outcast and the lawless American frontier as a woman. As much potential as she has as a vampire, her beginnings leave her weak and at the mercy of far more powerful forces. It is with intelligence and true grit that she must learn to survive and thrive.

But the real struggle for Ariane is to maintain her sense of honor and humanity as she fights against the demands of her nature and the madness of her bloodline. While far from a warrior of light, she is fearless when she chooses to fight for what she believes in and builds bonds of deep friendship with interesting and diverse people. Her acts of kindness are rare, but they shine as genuine and without the avarice and cruelty inherent to her kind.

While she definitely stumbles at times, Ariane remains steadfast to her friends and an anti-hero to those she saves along the way. I hope that her journey keeps her from succumbing to wickedness and allows her to emerge as something special. A dark star in a world of darkness.

title: Great Little Toy for Older Children and Adults
text:
I have been a fan of toy steam engines since I received a German made WILESCO engine for Christmas in 1961! This little engine by SunnyTech, a Chinese company, is very well made, with all brass parts, except for an O-ring to seal the boiler. When I first fired the engine up it ran like who-shot-john! I was rather amazed. This will make a great gift for any budding engineers that you may know, or any professional engineers, for that matter.
There are some pitfalls that the buyer should be aware of:
There are no instructions, at least in the one I bought has no instructions, just an exploded drawing showing how it should be put together. It is a good thing that I had experience with toy steam engines.
NEVER fill the boiler more than 2/3 full.
When running, it will spray some water, this is normal for a steam engine.
It does vibrate when running, place it on a stable surface.
The engine gets HOT when running. Take appropriate precautions.
Use alcohol as a fuel. Ethel or methyl alcohol (+95%) will work best. I tried 91% Isopropyl alcohol and it works fine, although it covered the boiler with soot. So you might want to avoid that.
NEVER use any petroleum derived fuel such as gasoline or Coleman fuel.
The engine is designed to only run for a few minutes on one boiler of water. Blow the lamp out immediately when the boiler is low on water or you may damage the engine with excess heat.
Remember, this is a toy but only for older children and adults.

title: Loved it!  Exciting, Danger, and Loads of Adventure.
text:
Katelin has found some peace and finds she looks forward to returning and spending the summer with her grandmother. Alone, without Simon, Katelin not only finds her own adventure but encounters a young man who sends flutters through her stomach. Through the journey, Katelin and her elfin friends discover how deeply her loyalty, fearlessness and determination runs. Together they must overcome the tyrant of the Elfin world and keep the Orb out of his grasp. The only question is, is Katelin strong enough or will she bite off more than she can handle?

What a fantastic fantasy! I enjoyed the first book but was blown away by the second. Sharon Dwyer set the "worlds" up very well, the characters were very well developed; Katelin was perfect! Dwyer captured Katelin’s "attitude" and emotional well-being accurately. Dwyer skillfully wrote the stories so that her readers do/will connect with Katelin in one way or another. The connection between the worlds was realistically done - meaning the characters had believable crossover and purpose. The first book was excellent!

The second book, I LOVED! I enjoy reading books where the female character is strong without knowing it. Piney, while not a cute character in real life, became adorable and perfect for Katelin. Dwyer expertly built up the suspense between the two books and the characters. I am intrigued on how Nana and the other worlds play out in Katelin's birthright ... I suspect a twist somewhere!

Dwyer’s The Fastasmagorical Forest series is exciting, inviting and mesmerizing. Once you get into the books, there is no stepping away. Lots of fun, plot twists, and adventure.

Very well done! While a book for young adults, those of us who enjoy fantasy, magic and adventure will love this book as well! I cannot wait for the series to continue!!!

text:
I'm extremely impressed at the South Pacific book by LP. Sometimes with books that are published as multi-country guides, you're worried that they're going to totally miss the smaller islands that themselves don't warrant their own individual books. To my surprise, places like Niue, Tuvalu, Pitcairn Island (itself a curious choice) were covered and yet misses Nauru and Palau.

However, nitpicking aside, this is a really good book, even for travel book standards. It's pretty comprehensive, and you can tell that the book had boots on the ground instead of less dubious LP authors just writing about what they find on the internet.

As someone who likes to find a brand of travel books and stick with them, I feel that Lonely Planet fell apart over the last few years and are slowly getting back to the top of the heap. I plan to use this book as the primary source of information for Fiji and Tuvalu for starters, and then see where the winds take me. I'm happy with a travel book for once, and that says a lot.

Becc grew up in sunny California and always wanted to be a journalist. She and her two best friends, Eric and Serra, grew up dreaming of their future selves and passions. A clandestine relationship with an older man, Cal, separates Becc from the others, and the lies that follow threaten their friendship. Becc and Eric always seemed to have "something more," but the timing always seemed off.

Set in the late 90s and 2008, this novel goes back and forth between past and present. The references to an early dial-up internet world brought me right back to that time, and I loved the references- especially since Becc wants to be a journalist in a time when print journalism is going away. The contrasts between Southern and Northern California life was fun to read, and though the book started a little slowly, I really enjoyed the way the story picked up. Frog Lube has become the number one CLP that I use. I use the solvent only on the interior of the barrel as needed. One of the nice things about Frog Lube CLP is that it smells like wintergreen. While I love the smell of Hoppes in the morning, everyone else in the house would complain. I did a lot of research as to the protective capabilities of different lubes. One video posted by a you tuber with way too much time on his hands (but I thank him) showed long term corrosion testing of a bunch of products. Of all the products, Frog Lube and WD 40 Extreme Corrosion Protection had metal test samples soaked in corrosive for months free of any corrosion. I do not recommend any penetrating oil or corrosion preventative on a firearm. Too many chances that it will penetrate a cartridge or primer. Frog Lube is non-toxic and works well. title: A Treasure Trove of Storytelling, Memorable Characters, and Rugged Beauty
text: This is a grand, sweeping, cinematic and sensitive novel about explorations into unmapped Alaskan territory in the 1880s led by a U.S. Army colonel. Concurrent with Col. Forrester's adventure is that of his young wife Sophie, who remains behind at Vancouver Barracks, and takes it upon herself to buck tradition and study the science and art of photography. She is a pioneer in a world where women's lives and roles have long been conscribed; a woman who seeks her own purpose and work, following her love of birds into a means of recording their beauty (and enduring the agonizing months of waiting for her husband's return). The story is told through journal entries, letters, new articles, and excerpts from historical documents which span the time period from the 1880s to the present. Each voice is distinct, credible, and unique. The descriptions of scenery are breathtaking and vivid. One feels the hunger and deprivations, as well as the sweeping grandeur and awe of the terrain, and trepidation surrounding occurrences which defy description. The explorers meet Native peoples who have never before seen white men, yet sense them to be harbingers of ineluctable change. The hardcover contains a treasure trove of illustrations, a magnificent map and many beautiful qualities - well worth the price, as I plan to cherish this book and lend it to trusted friends.

title: A Concise & Well-Written Treatise on Freedom.
text:
This thin book is packed with common sense about politics and freedom. And although I knew most of the positions Ron Paul supports and the evidence for them, I still learned some new things.

My favorite quote from the entire book: "Truth is treason in the empire of lies." Oh man, that's a zinger. And it describes our current political environment perfectly.

My only criticism of the book is minor: He brings up the issue of 9/11 briefly, but speaks as if terrorists were solely responsible for it. I suppose the book would've gotten way off track if he had mentioned it, but there's plenty of evidence that 9/11 was an inside job. And I'm not only referring to "Loose Change." (Take Robin Hordon's testimony, for instance, among many others.)

If we don't make changes, we're bound for tough times ahead. This quote from the book sums up well where we're headed:

"Any government that inflates the money supply runs the risk of hyperinflation, which occurs when the money supply is increased so much as to render the currency completely worthless. [...] The textbook case in the twentieth century took place in Germany in 1923. [...] The result was the complete ruin of the German mark, which German children began gluing together to make kites and German adults burned in order to keep warm." (p. 150-151)

In fact, he was downright distraught while sitting on the counter and he flopped around in our hand making it difficult to use. We then stumbled on the Lunatec. Yes, it's a little different. Like a dish cloth but ...more...nylon-netty and flimsy. But that's what makes it perfect! The Luncatec can lay across a finger tip and wipe inside a water bottle or other small area, lay flat and wash out a large water trough or bowl, or, fold it in half or quarters for a scrub-pad effect. A Scrub Buddy, with average use (used twice a day on 6 bowls) lasted about 2 weeks. So far, the Lunatec has been here and after nearly 3 weeks, shows ZERO signs of wear. No smell, no scudge, no bacteria. Just clean, clean, scrubbing and clean clean bowls. Oh, we noted another reviewer was unhappy with the Lunatec because he said he washed out a bowl with bread dough and it clogged the Lunatec. Well, duh, or, should we say "Doh!" You should expect that result with ANY type of sponge or cloth and a gooey/gummy dough. When we make bread or macaroni and cheese and have gooey bowls, we use plastic pan scrapers or a hard sink brush to knock off all the gooey/gummy stuff first and then use a sponge or cloth to do the washing/sanitizing. One Scrub Daddy for $8.50 or FOUR (4) Lunatec's for $7.50. The choice is simple, we think. This product stands up, does MORE than it should, and for that, we love you, you Lunatec!

title: Original fantasy with strong world building and characters
text:
Full disclosure: I won this in a Goodreads giveaway.

It's very, very rare to come across a truly original entry in the epic fantasy world, these days. Though in some ways I'm not even sure fantasy describes this book. Yes, it's obviously fantasy with magic and different races and such things, but at the same time it doesn't seem to focus on those things. It doesn't have the 'feel' of a typical fantasy book, and to me that's a good thing. Perhaps because it lacks some of the heaviness that many serious fantasy novels have. I did find that to be a good thing, though. It let the story move fairly quickly without getting bogged down on small details.

The world itself is very well laid out, especially because the reader is discovering it as the main character does. Rather clever of the author, there. Didn't even occur to me as I was reading, but in retrospect it worked and was very entertaining.

Characters...complex, interesting, well-rounded. I could go on, but you get the idea. At no point did I get the feeling I was dealing with cut outs or your typical fantasy cliches. Though I'll admit I'm a sucker for an anti-hero, which the main character definitely is. The relationships throughout the story are just as interesting, and nothing is ever quite as it seems.

I found the story itself to be very compelling and very original. It was one of those books that I couldn't wait to pick up when I had to set it down to go do something else. Halfway through I found myself lamenting the fact that there aren't any other books in the series written yet. I'm not going to talk much about it because there really is a lot to give away. I, for one, did not see the twists coming.

I really look forward to the next book in the series and finding out more about these characters, as well as the world they live in. Unlike so many books, these days, there's a very satisfying ending to this tale. Yes, it's apparently part of a larger story arc, but the author has not neglected the necessary resolution in each smaller part.
